raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old male presented to the emergency room complaining of progressive dyspnea and productive cough over the course of 4 months. He also noted decreased appetite with a 50-pound weight loss over the past 5 months. He had no significant past medical or surgical history and was not taking any medications. His family history was unremarkable. He quit smoking tobacco two months ago due to worsening respiratory status; he rarely used alcohol and never used recreational drugs. He was unmarried and in a long-term heterosexual relationship and denied multiple sexual partners. He was currently working in an automobile parts factory as a janitor. After high school he had enlisted in the army and served for four years; at that time he was stationed in Hawaii. While in Hawaii he visited a single prostitute on several occasions.
Initial vital signs revealed temperature was 99.9 F, blood pressure 128/83 mmHg, pulse 134 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 22 breaths/minute; oxygen saturation was 92% on room air. He was in moderate respiratory distress, yet was awake, alert, and cooperative. Extraocular muscles were intact; there was no nystagmus or scleral icterus. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light. He had thrush under his tongue and on the palate. There was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Heart rate was regular with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops by auscultation. There were no palpable thrills. He had equal chest rise bilaterally. Breath sounds were diminished throughout, with rales and dullness to percussion in the lower lung fields bilaterally. Sensory and motor examination was grossly intact.
Laboratory data revealed white blood count 13,900/mcL, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 370,000/mcL, sodium 131 mmol/L potassium 5.8 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, carbon dioxide 17 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 155 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 8.9 mg/dL. Arterial blood gases showed a pH of 7.39, pCO2 32.2 mmHg, bicarbonate 19.1 mmol/L, and pO2 74.5 mmHg on 3 L nasal cannula. Chest X-ray showed diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities (Figure 1). He was found to be HIV positive with CD4 count of <5 cells/cc and viral load of 1,180,000 copies. Bronchoalveolar lavage was preformed; Grocott's methenamine silver stain of the washings demonstrated Pneumocystis jiroveci (Figure 2). He received antibiotics and steroids with gradual improvement.
On hospital day 14, he became confused and acutely developed nystagmus with both a horizontal and prominent vertical component. He was also found to have ataxia with finger to nose testing and difficulty sitting up without support. Considering his immunosuppressed state, infectious and neoplastic etiologies were the primary diagnostic considerations. Lumbar puncture revealed clear CSF, normal opening pressure, and normal cell counts. Polymerase chain reactions for Epstein-Barr virus, Herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, and John Cunningham (JC) virus were negative. Nontreponemal serological screening for syphilis (VDRL), toxoplasmosis antibody, and Cryptococcus antigen titers were negative. CT of the head did not show any intracranial mass, hemorrhage, or other acute findings. MRI of the brain revealed a slight increase in T2 signal within the medial aspect of thalamus bilaterally (Figure 3). After excluding infection and neoplasm, the clinical diagnosis of Wernicke's encephalopathy was made. Intravenous thiamine was administered resulting in resolution of symptoms, which confirmed the diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old male presented with a 4-month history of progressive dyspnea and productive cough, accompanied by decreased appetite and a 50-pound weight loss over 5 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy, the patient developed progressive shortness of breath, productive cough over 4 months, and anorexia with a 50-pound weight loss over 5 months. Following admission, diagnosis of AIDS and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and gradual respiratory improvement on antibiotics and corticosteroids, he acutely developed confusion, horizontal and prominent vertical nystagmus, finger-to-nose dysmetria, and truncal ataxia on hospital day 14.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known prior medical or surgical history. Social history: factory janitor, former US Army soldier stationed in Hawaii for 4 years (visited a female commercial sex worker several times while in Hawaii), currently in a long-term heterosexual relationship; quit smoking tobacco 2 months prior due to dyspnea, rare alcohol use, no illicit drug use. Family history unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 4 months of progressive dyspnea and productive cough, 5 months of anorexia and 50-pound weight loss, oral thrush, and hospital day 14 acute confusion, oscillopsia/nystagmus, and gait/truncal ataxia. No home medications.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: temperature 99.9 °F, blood pressure 128/83 mmHg, heart rate 134 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, SpO2 92% on room air; awake, alert, in moderate respiratory distress; intact extraocular movements without nystagmus or icterus; sublingual and palatal oral thrush; no lymphadenopathy; regular tachycardia without murmurs; diminished breath sounds throughout with bibasilar rales and dullness to percussion; intact baseline neurological exam. Hospital day 14 neurological exam: acute confusion, horizontal and prominent vertical nystagmus, dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing, and severe truncal ataxia (unable to sit unsupported).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: WBC 13,900/mcL, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 370,000/mcL, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, CO2 17 mmol/L, BUN 155 mg/dL, serum creatinine 8.9 mg/dL; ABG on 3 L nasal cannula: pH 7.39, pCO2 32.2 mmHg, bicarbonate 19.1 mmol/L, pO2 74.5 mmHg. Chest X-ray showed diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities. HIV test positive.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was <5 cells/mm3 and plasma HIV viral load was 1,180,000 copies/mL. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain demonstrated Pneumocystis jirovecii. Day 14 lumbar puncture showed clear CSF with normal opening pressure and normal cell counts; CSF PCRs for EBV, HSV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and JC virus were negative, and VDRL, Toxoplasma antibody, and Cryptococcus antigen titers were negative. Head CT was negative for mass or hemorrhage; brain MRI revealed symmetric mild T2 hyperintensity in the bilateral medial thalami.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with newly identified advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 <5 cells/mm3, HIV viral load 1,180,000 copies/mL), Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (confirmed on BAL GMS stain), severe renal failure, and non-alcoholic Wernicke's encephalopathy on hospital day 14 (confirmed by classic triad of confusion, horizontal/vertical nystagmus, and ataxia, bilateral medial thalamic T2 hyperintensity on brain MRI, exclusion of CNS opportunistic infections including CMV, EBV, HSV, JCV, Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, and neurosyphilis on CSF analysis, and rapid clinical resolution following parenteral thiamine). Treated with antibiotics and corticosteroids for PJP and intravenous thiamine for Wernicke's encephalopathy with complete resolution of neurological symptoms.
